newsitem.title: FRANCE: French teachers strike in job cuts protest.
newsitem.headline: French teachers strike in job cuts protest.

text.p: French teachers went on strike on Monday, forcing hundreds of schools to close and disrupting others in a one-day protest over government plans to shed some 2,300 education jobs.

Teaching unions, which planned demonstrations in some 60 cities and towns with the biggest march due in Paris, claimed victory a few hours into the school day with an estimate that more than 80 percent of primary school teachers followed their strike call.

More than 2,000 teachers marched through the southwestern city of Bordeaux in late morning while most other demonstrations were planned for the afternoon, including one in Paris which aimed at marching on the education ministry.

The stoppage was the first in four years called jointly by the country's five biggest teachers' unions, which represent some 825,000 teachers. They advised parents not to take their children to school.

The Syndicat des Enseigants union said in a statement that, in the secondary sector, the strike rallied 70 percent of teachers in junior high schools and close to 60 percent of teachers in high schools.
A spokeswoman for the education ministry put the number of strikers at 59 percent in the primary sector, 44 percent in secondary schools and 20 percent among non-teaching personnel.
Several hundred schools were forced to close, she said.

"By participating massively in the strike, the teachers are showing their determination to make the government change its policy, especially on jobs and budget issues," said Herve Baro, secretary-general of the Syndicat des Enseignants.
The government has announced plans to eliminate more than 5,000 jobs in primary and secondary education in 1997 as a result of dropping birthrates in recent years.
Some 2,700 new posts will be created in higher education but teachers say that will still mean 2,300 fewer jobs in their profession.

The government, under fire for its budget and economic policies after unemployment reached a record 12.6 percent last month, will be closely watching the teachers as a measure of national dissatisfaction with the programme of Prime Minister Alain Juppe.
Labour leaders have been predicting significant unrest in the coming months and a big civil service strike has been set for October 17.
Marc Blondel, leader of Force Ouvriere, one of France's three biggest unions, accused Juppe of failing to stay in touch with union federations.

"Since October of last year, Juppe's labour affairs adviser hasn't called me once. When you lead a country you have to be in touch with those who represent part of that country," Blondel, told Europe-1 radio.

Opinion polls show Juppe's popularity ratings at near-record lows, and some deputies in the governing centre-right have begun openly pleading for a change in priorities well ahead of 1998 general elections.

But so far there has been little evidence of dissatisfaction of the magnitude that led to last year's crippling public sector strikes, which virtually paralysed France for a four-week period during November and December.
In a separate protest, train drivers at state-owned SNCF struck on Monday in a protest at working hours in the eastern suburbs of Paris, cutting services by a third.
